extracted.intended_audience: inventors (non-lawyers) who want to draft or participate in drafting provisional and utility patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for inventors on preparing, organizing, and drafting provisional and utility U.S. patent applications (including what to include, how to search prior art, how to work with a patent attorney, and basic claim-drafting principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and legal effect of a provisional application
rubrics_metrics.description: A provisional application is a summary of an idea (with drawings, graphs, photos, test data optional) filed with the PTO that is never examined; its only legal effect is to provide a filing date that can be claimed by a later utility application filed within one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File a provisional quickly to secure an early filing date; include as much technical detail as desired (drawings, photos, flowcharts). The provisional will receive a serial number (e.g., 60/123,456) and filing date. The utility must state the provisional number and claim the provisional priority within 1 year to get the priority date printed on the issued patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional drafting strategy: clarity, breadth, and avoid claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional applications should be written clearly, strongly, and broadly; claims are not required and are typically omitted to keep the provisional nimble and less attackable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on making the technical summary reliable and convincing rather than attempting carefully drafted claims. Avoid putting claims in a provisional unless you have good reason—claims can invite early attack and criticism. Tone should be cautious ('I think this might be a good idea...') rather than grandiose assertions of entitlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain the benefit of a provisional filing date, the same inventor must file a utility application within one year and the utility must state the provisional's number and claim its priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing the 1-year deadline forfeits the provisional's priority. Plan follow-up filings early and track deadlines carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a standard utility application format
rubrics_metrics.description: A time-honored sequence of headings for a utility application (Title; Government Support; Field of the Invention; Background of the Invention; Summary of the Invention; Brief Description of the Drawings; Detailed Description; Examples; References; Claims) should be followed unless there's a good reason to alter it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting each major section on a new sheet can make later edits easier. Subheadings may be added for clarity. The standard format helps attorneys, examiners, and docketing clerks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The title should be short (original advice: fewer than about eight words) and serves only as a finding aid; it does not restrict patent coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep titles concise and informative. (Note: later update mentions PTO allows longer titles but still advises brevity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Government support disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a Government Support heading only if government funding was used; otherwise omit it; if used, indicate the funding agency (grant number optional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide required government funding information to avoid obligation issues or false statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: List a broad field of technology (e.g., chemistry, electronics) and then cite a more specific field or goal (e.g., 'drugs for treating XYZ syndrome').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section helps PTO docket clerks assign the application to the appropriate art unit; it is not crucial to patent scope but aids administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background of the invention — contextual essay
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a short essay (suggested two to five pages, double-spaced) describing the field so an intelligent non-specialist will understand the context and significance of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain important terms, distinctions, and substitute terminology; avoid bare dictionary definitions; cite standard textbooks or review articles for further context. Use this section to create a good first impression with non-expert readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background of the invention — prior art analysis (three-paragraph format)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each important piece of prior art, prepare three short paragraphs: (1) summary of the prior art (how it works), (2) factual description of its limitations, and (3) why the new invention is different and better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staple the three-paragraph analysis to a copy of each prior art item and give them to the attorney; this saves time and money and helps prepare stronger responses to later examiner rejections. Point to exact pages/columns/lines in patents when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background of the invention — objectives/goals listing
rubrics_metrics.description: List the objects and objectives of the invention (e.g., 'One object is to create a simple, inexpensive, durable hyper widget with fewer moving parts…').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly articulating objectives frames the invention's advantages and supports claim drafting and prosecution arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a brief (one page or less) overview intended for readers unfamiliar with the invention; include what it is, how it is used, and why it's useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a map for readers; be able to give a 3–5 minute verbal overview. The Summary is often repeated as the Abstract and will be widely read in data services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brief description of the drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide figure legends that concisely identify views (e.g., 'Figure 1 is a plan view showing the hyper widget of this invention'), and include drawings such as line drawings, graphs, flow-charts, plasmid maps, chromatographs, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings do not include tables. Photographs are generally discouraged for printing but may be submitted to the examiner. Give the attorney copies of prior art drawings labeled as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings quality and submission practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Make drawings large, clear, and filling at least two-thirds of a sheet; provide two copies—one 'plain vanilla' unlabeled and one labeled with component names and notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the labeled copy, put labels around the edges and use arrows. Don't assign call-out numbers yourself—the attorney will do that later. Informal drawings or computer-generated drafts are acceptable for filing to save time and cost; formal drawings can be created after allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a narrative explanation of the invention—how it works and, for mechanical/electrical inventions, an explanation of the figures; for chemical/biological inventions, explain steps and include Examples as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal the best mode known at filing and anticipate possible modifications ('alternate preferred embodiment'). Use functional language where appropriate with one or two examples (e.g., 'means for attaching part A to part B').

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor must disclose the 'best mode of carrying out the invention' known on the filing date; hiding the best mode while using an inferior version to obtain a patent can lead to invalidation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be fully forthcoming with the best version at filing. Improvements discovered after filing can be kept as trade secrets and disclosed in later filings if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and disclosure of negative or unsuccessful data
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors and attorneys must act with candor and good faith in bringing all relevant information to the examiner; concealing unsuccessful experiments, negative data, or prototypes can invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring all data to the patent attorney and clearly point out best mode and unsuccessful results; the attorney can advise on presentation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / Examples requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For chemical and biological inventions (and where necessary elsewhere), include Examples with enough detail and data to allow 'someone with ordinary skill in the art' to repeat the experiment and obtain successful results without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify suppliers (with city), model numbers, trademarks, purity, product codes, and any deviations from published methods. If biological materials are not publicly available, consider deposit with a public depository. Describe quantities and exact procedures used.

rubrics_metrics.name: References and citations practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If abbreviated citations are used in-text (e.g., 'Smith 1980'), provide full citations (including titles) in a References section in alphabetical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete citations help examiners and future readers locate prior art and contextual literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: fundamental role and basic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the inventor's property; anything described but not claimed becomes public. Two basic rules: (1) every 'limitation' in a claim must be infringed for that claim to be infringed; (2) infringement of any claim constitutes infringement of the entire patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including non-essential limitations in independent claims. Each limitation should either define the invention or avoid prior art. Draft several independent claims from different angles; use dependent claims to recite optional features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-drafting strategy and inventor involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim drafting is specialized and inventors are advised not to draft claims themselves, but they should understand claim basics and actively review and question attorney-drafted claims to ensure maximum protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After attorney drafts claims, study every word to see if words can be removed while maintaining distinction from prior art. Insist on explanations from the attorney for phrasing choices; a good attorney will engage collaboratively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes any publicly available information as of the filing date—patents, journal articles, textbooks, catalogs, brochures, ads, manuals, foreign publications, translations, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search broadly and include anything that resembles, bears on, describes components of, or shows attempts to solve the same problem. Obtain translations for foreign items when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art search practice and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors should do an initial prior art search and obtain three clean copies of the most relevant prior art (one for the inventor's file, one for the attorney, one for submission with the application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use databases such as the USPTO, Delphion (historically), esp.espacenet.com, pctgazette.wipo.int, and scientific literature databases (e.g., PubMed/Entrez) for non-patent literature. If paying for a professional search, ask which databases were searched. Keep copies organized and labeled to save attorney time and fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of databases and field-specific resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Different fields have specialized resources (e.g., National Library of Medicine, PubMed, MESH terms) and university librarians/reference specialists can help locate literature and do cost-effective searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult field experts and specialized libraries; for biotechnology, know about NLM and depositary processes. Librarians may perform lower-cost searches than commercial searchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and figures: what to include and printing considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings can include line drawings, graphs, flow-charts, plasmid maps, DNA/amino acid sequences, chromatographs; photographs are usually avoided in printed patents but may be shown to attorneys/examiners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sketches even if informal; machine-generated small strip charts should be inked to convert to reproducible black-and-white drawings. Study drawings in the same field to learn conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing with informal drawings to save cost/time
rubrics_metrics.description: If in a hurry, file with informal drawings (inventor- or attorney-drawn) or computer-generated drafts; formal drafts by a professional draftsman can be prepared after allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal drawings are acceptable to avoid delay and expense; if the application is not allowed, you avoid the cost of professional drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication and organization for working with an attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors should be actively involved: know relevant prior art, provide organized writeups (three-paragraph prior-art analyses), and expect the utility application to be reviewed by a patent attorney before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-organized inventor saves attorney time and money. Challenge and question attorney choices; a collaborative relationship benefits prosecution and claim strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style: clarity and audience awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are written for four types of readers—(1) technical specialists, (2) patent examiners, (3) judges, and (4) patent attorneys/licensing readers—so the best approach is plain, clear, methodical English and avoidance of legalistic jargon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases like 'the hereinbefore mentioned component.' Explain background and terms for non-specialists and be methodical so all four audiences can understand the invention.
